extracted.intended_audience: media creators, comedy writers, game designers, performers and fans looking for examples/techniques for humorous or gag credits
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and examples for creating humorous, unexpected, or interactive end/credit sequences across media (films, games, theatre, radio, webcomics, albums). Shows many techniques—fake roles, interruptions, interactive credits, meta-jokes—to make credits themselves a comedic element.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit non-human or unexpected entities
rubrics_metrics.description: List software, animals, pets, or other non-people as performers or contributors instead of (or alongside) actual humans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vane Lily credits the software used for vocals; Zappa albums credit dogs Bing Jang and Arkansas; LucasArts games credit designers' cats; Telltale Games lists 'Telltale Pets'. Use for absurdity, commentary, or in-joke; can be used as retaliation (replacing real credits with pets) or to underline a theme (dehumanization, satire).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use fake/spoof names and spoof personae
rubrics_metrics.description: Give credited people spoofed, punny, or parody names rather than actual names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Castlevania spoof names (Christopher Bee, Mix Shrecks), prank call names on Car Talk (Dewey, Cheatum and Howe), ROM hack credits listing 'Me' repeatedly. Effective for playful tone; avoid targeted real-person insults unless deliberately satirical and safe/legal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assign comedic or exaggerated job titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace ordinary credit titles with humorous, grandiose, or theme-fitting job descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Diabolical Design' on playfield, 'Astigmatic One Eyed Typography Institute', 'Torture Innovator', 'Mortal Control Expert' (Immortals Fenyx Rising). Use thematic titles to extend a joke or world-build; can be as simple as inserting a nickname in quotes (John 'Night Train' Goff).

rubrics_metrics.name: Insert fake bios or fake playbills before/among real ones
rubrics_metrics.description: Include intentionally ridiculous, invented cast bios or playbill entries either as lead-in or interleaved with real credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spamalot's fake cast bios and fake playbill about Finland; If/Then insert 'Adele Dazeem' fake bio. Use to set comedic tone before the real list; ensure distinction so audience sees it's a gag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrupt credits with action or resume the story during credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Stop the credits to continue the game/story (boss fight, scene continuation) or have characters interrupt the credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bayonetta interrupts credits to continue the story; Metal Gear Solid 4 plays a scene mid-credits; Monkey Island stops credits so player can continue. Useful for surprise and to subvert 'end' expectations; must be timed for audience effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make credits interactive or part of gameplay
rubrics_metrics.description: Turn the credits into an interactive segment: clickable elements, playable mini-challenges, destructible letters, or unlockable secret endings tied to credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bayonetta playable flashback photos, Jaleco destructible-letter credits (score points), Punch-Out!! mini-game during credits for points, Tetris: The Grand Master requiring play behind credits. Interactive credits reward attentive players and extend engagement but require extra design effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use credits to reflect episode/theme or act as additional joke content
rubrics_metrics.description: Tailor the credits' wording or structure to mirror or comment on the episode's theme, often producing additional jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Jeremy Hardy Speaks to the Nation credits reflecting episode themes; This American Life credits a staffer with a random quote from the episode. Use to extend narrative voice and reinforce theme; keep jokes concise to avoid diluting effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Break the fourth wall or directly address the audience in credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Have credits tell the audience to do something or verbally acknowledge the viewer/reader in a meta way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Secret of Monkey Island tells players to get off the computer and go to bed; credits thanking the player for reading. This produces intimacy and meta-humor but can feel condescending if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use running-gag voiceovers/commentary over credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Overlay the credits with character commentary, snark, or a recurring voice gag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Crash Bandicoot commentaries, Kang and Kodos snarking in Simpsons games, Murray's wisecracks during Tales of Monkey Island credits. Works well when established characters/voices can lampoon the credits themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberately omit or 'blank' parts of credits for comedic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave pictures blank or omit expected information to produce a visible joke (e.g., invisible character's art is blank).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: D&D Monster Manual: blank artwork for invisible stalker but credit still given. Use sparingly — the gap between expectation and absence creates humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody legal disclaimers and standard boilerplate in credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Mimic or subvert legal text, safety disclaimers, or corporate boilerplate for comedic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Pajama Sam's bogus 'No Animals Were Harmed', Darkside Detective parodies legal disclaimers, Portal 2's redacted Notice of Dismissal. Parodying formal language can be hilarious if it highlights absurdity; be careful with real legal wording to avoid misrepresentation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit fictional companies/entities/persons
rubrics_metrics.description: Include obviously fictional sponsors, companies, or entities in the credits list for humor or world-building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Deathball 2000™ in attract mode, Pony Island's stock historical villains listed in credits, 'Happy Nightmare Corporation' in Second Reality Project. Useful for extending the fictional universe or satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format credits as themed lists or non-standard categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Replace conventional sections with themed lists (e.g., 'Things That Are Cool/Not Cool', 'Things That Explode') or other creative groupings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Power Pete lists 'Things That Are Cool/Not Cool/Things That Explode'. This subverts the expectation of dry role lists and invites comedic associations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give characters or in-world roles honorary/absurd titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Award ludicrous, ceremonious, or hyperbolic titles to characters or creators in credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Legend of Kyrandia credits narrator with royal-sounding long title; Immortals Fenyx Rising credits Zeus with extravagant roles. Amplified titles can satirize ego or heroic tropes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-deprecating or blunt 'not very involved' credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly downplay contributions in credits (e.g., 'not terribly involved in this project actually').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Cannon Fodder 2 credit to Chris Yates as 'not terribly involved in this project actually.' Such honesty can be endearing or funny — use if tone fits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hide secret/unlockable credits accessible by easter-egg actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Conceal special credit sequences revealed only by secret inputs or hidden actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Stern Pirates secret flipper button to show pirate credits; secret endings exposing gag credits. These reward exploration and fandom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use layout, alignment, and typography as part of the joke
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit formatting (misalignment, ASCII terminal look, backward text) to create visual gags in the credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Baba Is You misaligned credits, Portal's ASCII terminal-style lyrics, credits that rewind or glitch. Visual treatments can enhance comedic effect but must remain legible enough to recognize the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Embed inside jokes and creator references in credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Populate credits with in-group references, merchandise plugs, or private jokes that reward attentive fans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: D&D references to pantaloons of deities, Paranoia's 'Your Mother' credit, special thanks to niche friends. Inside jokes strengthen community but may alienate outsiders if overdone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat or multiply a single credit entry humorously
rubrics_metrics.description: List the same person multiple times with incremental variations (Me, Me Again, Me Again Again) to emphasize a sole creator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Super Bobido World ROM hack credit list ('Me', 'Me Again', etc.). This is useful for small solo projects or parodying over-crediting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use interruptions, corpsing, or cast reactions during credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Have cast members react to credits being read (stumbling on names, corpsing, entering accents) to create live-comedy effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Navy Lark announcers cut off or corrected, actors corpsing in background. This feels organic in audio/recorded formats and underscores comedic performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stage a fake ending during credits to extend or subvert the finale
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the credits appear to be the true ending (failure screen, fake scoring) before revealing the real continuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Curse of Monkey Island fakes a game-over then resumes; many games present 'fake' scoring/credits before continuing. This misdirection is gratifying when revealed and can be used to reward curiosity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody or lampoon 'special thanks' and sponsor lists
rubrics_metrics.description: Fill special thanks with absurd, irrelevant, or celebrity names for comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Afterlife includes Von Trapp family and Janeane Garofalo; Digimon World thanks 'chicken nuggets'. Use to satirize credit boilerplate and fandom name-dropping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misattribute roles to famous or unexpected people for humor
rubrics_metrics.description: Assign surprising endorsements or unusual responsibilities to well-known names in the credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Star Wars Episode I: Racer credits Tim Schafer with 'Never Actively Tried to Sabotage the Project'; listings of celebrities in gag roles. This can be meta-humorous but avoid creating defamatory impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use credits as a storytelling device to advance plot or reveal scenes
rubrics_metrics.description: Embed scenes, revelations, or narrative developments into or immediately after credits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Bayonetta reveals threats during credits; Metal Gear Solid 4 plays a scene mid-credits; Portal's post-credits annotations add story. This turns credits into an active narrative space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make credits deliberately unreadable/rapid to create a gag
rubrics_metrics.description: Scroll credits so quickly, misalign them, or otherwise speed them up to be comically unreadable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Homestar Runner April Fools' fake credits going by too fast; NieR: Automata fake endings with impossibly fast credits. This can amuse but may frustrate players who want to read real credits—consider alternate accessible mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include gag nicknames, middle names, or 'training' credits
rubrics_metrics.description: Insert joke middle names, nicknames in quotes, or fictional training credits ('Weasel Training').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Normy's Beach gives fake middle names and 'Weasel Training'; many tabletop books include nicknames in credits. Small personal touches often land well in close-knit creative contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use credits to satirize industry practices or social commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Employ credit choices (e.g., crediting software) to make a statement about commodification, labor, or production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Vane Lily credits software to comment on dehumanization of minor internet celebrities. Credits can be a subtle platform for critique when aligned with the work's themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credit in-world characters with production roles
rubrics_metrics.description: List fictional characters (or the work's internal figures) as though they performed production tasks or staff roles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Discworld credits Terry Pratchett with 'Shouting At People' and similar in-world roles; Love, Ghostie credits 'Ghostina Aghoulera' as Lead Mentor. This reinforces world-building and humor simultaneously.
